rules_evaluated.evidence: Per content-strategy-agentic-engineering-101.md §Supplementary material and §M5-in-detail §Pre-reads before M5, this file is wired as one of the M4→M5 pre-reads, read while M4's un-packaged send-off is still running (also re-offered as optional M5 prep in learn-from-the-test.md L11). M4's mood is 'curious readiness' ('I've built enough to try something; let's see what the agent does with it') and M5's is 'learning through contrast'. The essay's own arc — early excitement (L9, 'AI can write code. A lot of code. Fast.') → the mercury problem, local success/global drift (L17-21) → 'Clean Code becomes steering' (L27-29) as the discipline that would have constrained that drift — hands the student exactly the open question the strategy doc says this pre-read slot owns ('what would have constrained the drift?', quoted verbatim in run-the-first-experiment.md L80) without naming M5's specific three-pattern (checked under §4 below). Student leaves this piece holding a general-purpose reframe (classic quality discipline = steering, not tidiness) rather than a resolved answer — it primes M5's 'learning through contrast' without pre-empting it. Mood is honored, not flattened.

This slot's mood is 'curious readiness' / 'learning through contrast', not 'unease' by name, but the essay's central tension (the mercury problem) is the closest content to the epistemic/punitive line this rule polices. L19: 'the code feels compliant, but the system is not yet trustworthy' — this frames a not-yet-known state about the SYSTEM, not a verdict on the student, who at this point in the arc hasn't sent anything off themselves. L17 attributes the drift to the agent ('the agent may agree, apologize, and still drift'), never to the reader. No line frames the coming M4/M5 experience as something the student will have gotten wrong; the frame throughout is 'here's what to watch for', which is not-knowing, not having-done-wrong. Stays inside.
